title: Gustafson v. Alloyd Co. (1995)
summary: A private stock purchase agreement is not a "prospectus" under section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, because "prospectus" must carry the same meaning throughout the Act and refers to a document soliciting the public to buy securities from an issuer.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 1995. Key line: "The 1933 Act, like every Act of Congress, should not be read as a series of unrelated and isolated provisions." (Justice Kennedy)

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Gustafson, McLean and Butler, who in 1989 were the sole shareholders of Alloyd, Inc. and sold the company. The respondents were the buyers: Wind Point Partners II, L.P., and the newly formed company that took the Alloyd Co. name after the sale. The buyers sued the sellers for rescission of the contract under section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, arguing that the contract of sale itself was a "prospectus" containing material misstatements. Gustafson answered that a prospectus means a communication soliciting the general public to buy securities from the original issuer, which a private negotiated sale is not.
sections.Material Facts: Gustafson decided in 1989 to sell Alloyd. Wind Point Partners agreed to buy substantially all of the outstanding stock, and on December 20, 1989 the parties executed a contract of sale. Wind Point agreed to pay $18,709,000 for the stock plus $2,122,219, a sum reflecting the estimated increase in Alloyd's net worth since the end of the previous year. The year-end audit then showed that Alloyd's actual 1989 earnings were lower than the estimates the parties had relied on in negotiating the adjustment. The buyers claimed that the sellers' statements about the company's financial data were inaccurate, making the contract's representations and warranties untrue, and that the contract was a prospectus so any misstatement in it triggered section 12(2).
sections.Procedural History: Alloyd Co. and Wind Point sued Gustafson and his co-shareholders in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois seeking outright rescission of the contract under section 12(2) of the 1933 Act. By the time the case reached the Supreme Court, the Court assumed that the stock purchase agreement contained material misstatements of fact by the sellers and that Gustafson could not carry his burden of proving due care, so the only question was whether the contract was a prospectus. Justice Kennedy wrote for a five-Justice majority holding that it was not. Four Justices dissented in two opinions.
sections.Issue: Whether the right of rescission that section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933 gives buyers against sellers who make material misstatements "by means of a prospectus or oral communication" extends to a private, secondary sale of stock, on the theory that the recitations in the written purchase agreement make the agreement a "prospectus" as defined in section 2(10) of the Act.
sections.Holding: No. The term "prospectus" must be read consistently throughout the Act. Section 10 requires a prospectus to contain the information in a registration statement, which only public offerings by an issuer or its controlling shareholders require, so a prospectus under section 10 is confined to documents related to public offerings. The same word in section 12 carries the same meaning. The section 2(10) definition, read as a whole with noscitur a sociis, refers to documents of wide public dissemination. A private contract of sale is not a prospectus, and section 12(2) gives the buyers no rescission claim.
sections.Reasoning: Kennedy began with section 10, not the definition. Section 10 says a prospectus "shall contain the information contained in the registration statement," and only public offerings by an issuer or its controlling shareholders require registration, so a section 10 prospectus is a public-offering document. Under the whole-act rule that identical words in one statute carry the same meaning, "prospectus" cannot mean one thing in section 10 and another in section 12. Turning to section 2(10), which defines a prospectus as "any prospectus, notice, circular, advertisement, letter, or communication, written or by radio or television," the Court rejected the buyers' reliance on the lone word "communication." Reading it to cover every writing would make "notice, circular, advertisement, [and] letter" surplusage, and noscitur a sociis, a word is known by the company it keeps, requires "communication" to match its neighbors, all documents of wide dissemination. "Prospectus" was a 1933 term of art for public solicitations. Justice Thomas, joined by Scalia, Ginsburg and Breyer, would have started with section 12(2) and the capacious section 2(10) definition: noscitur applies only to doubtful words, "communication" is a catchall, and the "unless the context otherwise requires" preface shows Congress expected the word to vary. Ginsburg, joined by Breyer, would start with the defining section.

topics.lrs-k-noscitur: The majority reads "communication" in section 2(10) in light of its listed neighbors, notice, circular, advertisement and letter, and confines it to public documents; Thomas replies that the canon applies only to words of doubtful meaning.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: Kennedy anchors the meaning of "prospectus" in section 10, which requires registration-statement contents, and carries that meaning into section 12 under the rule that identical words in one act mean the same thing.
topics.lrs-k-terms-of-art: The majority treats "prospectus" as a 1933 term of art for a document soliciting the public, which explains the partial circularity of the statutory definition and the no-reliance remedy.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: Both sides claim the text: the majority reads the whole act and the list in context, while the dissents insist the enacted definition in section 2(10) controls over structure and extrinsic meaning.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The opinions disagree about when a canon may be invoked, with Thomas charging that the majority used noscitur a sociis to manufacture ambiguity rather than resolve it.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 5 to 4. Justice Thomas dissented, joined by Justices Scalia, Ginsburg and Breyer: the section 2(10) definition is broad and unambiguous, noscitur a sociis cannot be used to create doubt where none exists, and the majority let section 10 become "the tail that wags the 1933 Act dog." Justice Ginsburg dissented separately, joined by Justice Breyer: interpretation of a defined term begins with the defining section, and the presumption of consistent meaning yields when a word serves different purposes in different provisions.
learning.why: The case teaches noscitur a sociis and the surplusage canon working together, and the whole-act presumption that a word means the same thing throughout a statute; the dissents show that these canons apply only when a term is ambiguous, and that a broad statutory definition can be read to override the ordinary or term-of-art meaning.
